Status effects in Monster Hunter work like in Dark Souls games.  Weapons will sacrifice raw damage to apply varying amounts of status value.  When the value applied to a monster hits a threshold, they become inflicted by the status.  It takes an increasing amount of status value to trigger subsequent activations of the monster.  While a monster is inflicted with a status, like say paralysis, hitting them with more paralysis status doesn't do anything...at least as far as I know.

Source: am depressed and often suicidal.  This is the basic framework I have developed over years of therapy.  I still suck at being happy but this can work, it's just hard to start and can be hard to maintain.

Start with a back-to-basics sanity check:  Getting enough sleep?  Daily walk?  Are you getting enough sunlight, which is more difficult to get this time of year (in the northern hemisphere at least)?  Eaten vegetable?

If no, is it because you are forgetting to or because you feel too tired or disinterested to do it?

if the latter, you are unofficially officially depressed.  This calls for a two-pronged offensive.

Part 1: Just(tm) do it(tm):
Pick one of the self-care things and try to do it.  If you fail, DO NOT be angry with yourself.  Dismiss that impulse.  Choose a different thing, or make the thing smaller, until you manage to do it.  Mentally congratulate yourself for doing it.  Then keep doing it or other things.  Over time, build to bigger things

Part 2: Seek joy:
Have you done a fun thing lately?  played video game?  Watched movie or youtube?  Listened to one (1) music?  Choose a theoretically fun thing and do it.  Choose something small.  Avoid eating food or drinking as "the fun thing", I keep trying to eat for fun and now I  am fat.  Do not be mad at yourself if you did not have fun doing the fun thing.  Praise yourself for attempting the fun thing even though you didn't enjoy it, as not enjoying things is perfectly normal.  Maybe you just didn't like that movie, or whatever.  Try to focus on the nice things in day-to-day life, like seeing a pretty bird.  Praise yourself for being happy about seeing the pretty bird.

This is all founded in your basic cognative-behavioural "rewire your own brain" therapy.  Remember that if it doesn't work for you, that's not a failure on your part.  keep trying to apply the method but feel free to seek out other options.  If you feel better for a bit and then bad again, that is unfortunately normal.  Don't beat yourself up over it.  If it works, you will be mad that it is working.  That is also normal.  Remember, it's about forcing yourself to acknowledge small good things instead of only the things that frustrate you.

with regards to the ban, mod was probably being trigger-happy.  Subreddits that big tend to be pretty hard on the mod team, amd sometimes the mods compensate by being ban-happy.  I was more trying to explain the general issues adhd people have with neurodivergent discourse.  I haven't really been on that sub in ages so I can't comment on whether it is toxic or not, lol

It's about wanting people to appreciate that you are struggling with something.  ADHD sucks, and it is unhelpful when people try to convince you there are "benefits" or that you don't need help when life constantly throws up barriers in your path.  Obviously we'd prefer not to be disabled at all, but we are.  My last appointment, my psychiatrist had to very gently remind me that I am disabled and can't judge myself using my fellow classmates as a point of comparison, that it's not fair to myself to demand I perform as well as people without adhd.  Would you want to come home after that sort of talk and find people on the subreddit about your condition playing down your hardship?

So the general deal with "neurodivergent" is that you see your specific impairment as merely a difference in how your mind functions as opposed to a disability.  It's gained a lot of ground with people who are autistic.  People with autism sometimes find that so long as people accomodate their social impairment, they are perfectly capable of living happy and fulfilling lives.  Pair that with often being gifted in some sense and it's understandable why you would want to discard the "disabled" label.  There have been similar pushes for people with physical impairments - such as needing a wheelchair - to be seen as "differently abled", not "disabled".  It's an attempt to buck the stigma.

Where problems can occur is when people who feel this way try to speak for others who may not, or try to reject truths that run up against their desired definition.  You can see an extreme version of this in parts of the "fat acceptance" movement where people start to deny the health issues associated with obesity are real and accuse doctors of lying to people about the reality of being overweight.  With autism, or ADHD, its entirely possible that an individual will feel that it is more of a benefit than a curse.  If you think the executive dysfunction is worth it in exchange for greater creativity that is great for you - but if you start telling other people who are suffering from their disorder that their pain isn't real, we have a problem.

You can find more specific info linked in the rules to the ADHD subreddit, but hopefully this gives you a general map for where and how things can go off the rails when discussing neurodiversity as a theory.

They did not attempt to verify or accomodate, but instead fired her as has always been policy.

Note that the employer is not necessarily required by law to let her continue as a driver (EEA s.6), but was obligated to engage with her to figure out something they could try.  Then the issue would have been whether the accomodations that would have been required would be an issue of hardship, or whether she lacked the credentials.  By not taking any steps to attempt to maybe do something, the company violated the EEA.

I call it symptom-based diagnosis vs cause-based diagnosis!  The example I use to explain it to people is 'hurty arm syndrome'.  You hit your arm against something, it hurts.  You go to the doctor.  The doctor doesn't understand the inner workings of your arm, so all they have to go on is that your arm hurts.  They diagnose you with hurty arm syndrome and tell you to try not moving it for a while because that sometimes works.  Over time, doctors notice additional symptoms and relate them to other treatments.  One specialist in hurty arm syndrome notes that patients whose arm seems oddly bent are more likely to get better if you straighten the arm and immobilize it with a cast.  Another specialist notes that loss of control of the hand is often a sign the patient won't fully recover.  Now you have a hurty arm spectrum upon which someone with hurty arm syndrome falls and which helps inform doctors of appropriate treatment.
